issues.title: DHCPv6 Sub-Options Format
issues.author: GIC-de
issues.body:
Bernie Volz from DHC Working Group proposes that the OPTION_RATE  DHCPv6 sub-options utilize a two-byte format for both the sub-option code and the sub-option length. This aligns sub-option formatting with the standard DHCPv6 option structure defined in RFC 8415, necessitating updates to existing text regarding minimum DHCPv6 option lengths.

While this approach introduces a structural difference between the corresponding OPTION_RATE DHCPv4 sub-options (which use single-byte fields) and OPTION_RATE  DHCPv6 sub-options, both protocols can continue to share the same registry of sub-option values. Standardizing on a uniform two-byte encoding/decoding structure for all DHCPv6 options simplifies implementation and eliminates the need for specialized parsing logic when introducing new options.

comments.author: GIC-de
comments.body: The draft version 01 now incorporates this topic.

issues.title: DHCPv4/v6 Code Points (TBD1 and 2)
issues.author: GIC-de
issues.body: Using a single placeholder (TBD1) for both the DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 option codes incorrectly implies that IANA will assign the identical numeric value to both. While this alignment is highly desired, it cannot be guaranteed during allocation. Therefore, this document should use distinct placeholders, TBD1 for DHCPv4 and TBD2 for DHCPv6, to avoid making assumptions. A note should been added to the IANA Considerations section requesting that IANA assign the same numeric value to both protocols if possible.

issues.title: Zero Length Options
issues.author: GIC-de
issues.body: We should consider to not allow 0-length options. If we decide to allow them, we need to document exactly how a 0-length option differs from simply omitting the option altogether. If there is a deliberate semantic difference between an absent option and a 0-length option in a response, we must explicitly define that behavior in the draft.

issues.title: Rate Conflicts
issues.author: GIC-de
issues.body:
In the current draft-00, the guidance for handling conflicting rate information between DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 states that clients "SHOULD apply the most recently received value". However, in dual-stack environments where DHCP transactions often complete asynchronously, this approach can easily lead to a race condition. Depending on which protocol finishes its transaction last, the applied rate could flap unpredictably between the two values.

To guarantee a deterministic state and prevent this flapping, we should update the draft to dictate a strict hierarchy. The primary recommendation is to mandate that clients SHOULD explicitly prefer the DHCPv6 rate over the DHCPv4 rate. 

Dictating a strict preference, however, introduces a new edge case regarding lease expirations that the draft needs to address. For instance, if a client prefers the DHCPv6 rate, we need to define what happens when that DHCPv6 lease expires while the DHCPv4 lease remains active. If the client simply retains the expired DHCPv6 rate indefinitely, the still-active DHCPv4 lease will never be able to step in and overwrite it.

To resolve this, clients should be required to store the learned rate alongside its source protocol. If the currently applied rate was sourced from DHCPv6 and that specific lease expires, the client needs to check if a valid DHCPv4 lease is still active. If it is, the active rate source effectively "demotes" to DHCPv4. While the applied rate itself temporarily remains the last value learned from DHCPv6, shifting the source ownership to DHCPv4 ensures that any subsequent DHCPv4 transactions can successfully update and overwrite that rate. On the other hand, if the preferred lease expires and there is no active secondary DHCPv4 lease to fall back on, the rate should simply reset to the device's default configuration.

comments.author: rpnz01
comments.body:
an alternative, lighter weight approach so that clients don't have to keep state yet still get stable and deterministic behaviour, is we set a rule based on the values rather than the address family.  i.e., clients SHOULD prefer the lower of the values.
This can be implemented with simple logic, rather than a lookup.

Now if we should prefer lower or higher, I don't know.  I think lower is safer?

comments.author: GIC-de
comments.body:
While implementing a simple rate comparison is straightforward, it is ineffective when actual line rates fluctuate over time. These variations are common and frequently stem from dynamic access adaptations (such as DSL synchronization changes), customer-initiated modifications to their service tiers, or ISP traffic-shaping policies that throttle bandwidth after a specific data volume is consumed.

Because rate updates via DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 occur independently, and bandwidth allocations can both increase and decrease, any heuristic that naively prefers the maximum or minimum reported rate will fail to accurately reflect the current state.

comments.author: rpnz01
comments.body:
In my head I was thinking those changes are intentional and should occur simultaneously across both address families in parallel under BAU operations, so we're only having to catch the fringe cases where they may not for some unplanned reason.

But yeah, whilst changes may get pushed to the server in parallel by the OSS, DHCP clients will only receive the updated information upon renew, and the lifetimes may be different between address families, plus the entropy with DHCPv6 means renews will always be skewed.   

Let's suggest the table to track idea and see what the WG thinks.

comments.author: moeller0
comments.body: I am all for act on all reports so "most recent report wins". It seems not too much to expect an ISP to feed both its DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 pathways with "ground truth" rate information, especially in the context of injecting that via a relay agent at e.g. the BNG. The protocol we invent here will not be fool-proof, so let's not make it more complicated by trying to solve competence issues at the ISP side (respectfully, I assume ISPs to get this right anyway). We could make it a MUST that both DHCP variants use the same ground truth information, on the basis of them not doing it will violate our protocol's assumptions.

comments.author: rpnz01
comments.body:
Thanks @moeller0.

I like the idea of specifying that they MUST be the same, with the justification that rates are not [usually] traffic managed individually per L3 address family.  There was also a comment from Ondrej at the mic, which I completely misunderstood, asking about should the two option values across the address families be summed together, we could fix that uncertainty at the same time.

The "most recent report wins", I'm still on the fence about.  I like the simplicity of it, but unsure about how non-deterministic it is, and  have historically seen issues when implementing traffic management based on TR-101's Option 82, depending on if DHCPv4 or DHCPv6 was used for authentication last.  But that was a combination of implementation issues / vendor support, that we should be designing this around.

I like the deterministic-ness of saying "in case of a discrepancy between address families, DHCPv6 option takes precedent", but could be swayed into the "most recent" camp.

comments.author: GIC-de
comments.body:
I tend to agree with the "most recent wins" approach. Temporary discrepancies between DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 are usually just expected transitional states during a rate change. Whichever protocol renews first will carry the new rate, so applying the most recently received value ensures the fastest application of updated rates.

If the network continuously sends different rates across the two address families, that is fundamentally a provisioning error. I am not convinced we need to enforce a strict mitigation strategy for handling misconfigured networks. Instead, we could propose a few valid strategies in the draft, but ultimately leave it to the implementation to choose the one that best fits their architecture.

From a practical implementation standpoint, "most recent wins" is often much easier to deploy. This is especially true for typical Linux-based stacks, where independent DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 daemons act asynchronously and simply trigger external scripts to apply rate information.

comments.author: moeller0
comments.body:
Considering the options I believe "most recent wins" is an acceptable compromise, as it naturally allows the timely rate changes some links might make desirable and keeps complexity at the CPE small, as there is little state to keep... if we want some help against misconfigurations we could recommend CPE to log the received rate information options for post-game analysis?
We could also explicitly note that the modell here is a unified L3-agnostic traffic shaper... and use SHOULDs so experimentally minded providers can still feel allowed to implement L3-aware shaper hierarchies if they feel like it.

comments.author: rpnz01
comments.body: Consider me won over to the "most recent wins" camp. :)

issues.title: Informational Rates
issues.author: GIC-de
issues.body:
Here, `MUST NOT` is incorrect; `SHOULD NOT` is a more appropriate choice, as CPE application remains possible.

```
If the rate type is set to 0, the explicitly signaled rates are
informational only.  Devices receiving this rate type MUST NOT apply
the specified rate limits to their physical interfaces, traffic
shapers, policers, or Active Queue Management (AQM) parameters. 
```

comments.author: GIC-de
comments.body: If the rate type is informational (0), it is considered to be L2 (default).

issues.title: PPP Authentication Reply
issues.author: GIC-de
issues.body:
Here, `MUST` is incorrect; `SHOULD` is a more appropriate choice, as CPE application remains possible.
```
If a client receives rate limits embedded within the PPP
authentication reply message and concurrently receives the DHCP
OPTION_RATE, the explicitly signaled DHCP OPTION_RATE MUST take
priority.  This precedence ensures that the standardized, dynamic
DHCP signaling supersedes fragmented or proprietary rate limits
previously negotiated during the PPP authentication phase.
```

comments.author: moeller0
comments.body: As written on-list, if we opt to go for "latest report takes precedence" this resolves organically...

comments.author: GIC-de
comments.body: Based on the discussion, I think it’s best to propose a recommended conflict resolution strategy rather than making it normative. This leaves room for CPE vendors to make it configurable or adapt their approach as field deployments evolve.

comments.author: moeller0
comments.body: Sure, a SHOULD with a short rationale to allow timely updates seems fine, or even just a MAY....

issues.title: Mandate L2-rate information, make L3-information an optional addition
issues.author: moeller0
issues.body: For the purpose of actually configuring CPE-side traffic shapers (required for allowing AQMs to actually be useful, when the interface egress rate exceeds the contracted bottleneck rate) the applicable gross L2-rate is necessary, so make that mandatory. L3-payload rates can be nice to report in that these could match closely to what end users see in capacity tests but make these second-class citizens here and mandate L2-rates. This might require a change in the options to always report L2 and L3 rates.

comments.author: GIC-de
comments.body: Let me provide some operational background behind the demand for L3 rates. The core issue goes both ways: you cannot perfectly convert L2 to L3 and vice versa because both require assuming an average packet size. While you could assume maximum frame size, the average packet size will likely be lower. So while most providers would likely prefer to apply an L2 rate, regulatory authorities in some countries strictly enforce L3 rates. In a large ISP I worked with, this went so far that the provider could not sell a 1000 Mbps product if the CPE lacked 2.5G ports, because a 1G physical port simply cannot deliver 1000 Mbps at L3 due to framing overhead. If a CPE cannot install L3 shapers directly, it needs to internally convert the rate based on its own local stack, accounting for its specific VLAN headers, PPPoE encapsulation, and other overhead. The default rate type remains L2 if not explicitly signaled, and the draft also allows clients to send a hint in their request if they prefer an L2 or L3 rate. That said, I see that this whole topic needs more detail in the draft, and we plan to clarify these mechanics in the next revision.

comments.author: moeller0
comments.body:
> you cannot perfectly convert L2 to L3 and vice versa because both require assuming an average packet size.

I respectfully beg to differ, knowing all applicable overhead (general and per-packet) I can very much deduce for a given L- packet how much transmission time it will consume on L2. My goal here is to make sure the proposed mechanism will include the required information tp make that happen.


> So while most providers would likely prefer to apply an L2 rate, regulatory authorities in some countries strictly enforce L3 rates.

I would argue providers opt for L2 rate shaping, as that is the only thing that makes sense given the reasons to traffic shape in the first place... And regulatory agencies might simply just want that advertised/contracted rates are communicated as easy to confirm in on-line speedtests TCP/HTTPS payload rates. I have yet to see a regulation requiring true L3-traffic shaping (see my example calculations how that would require an ISP to increase the L2-rate for smaller packets). The German regulatory agency (agreeing with BEREC guidelines) expects that the advertised maximum datarate is specified as L4-payload rate, but at the same time (also in agreement with BEREC) notes that this rate does not need to be the actual limit rate... So providers simply set their L2-shapers such that for the typical speedtest configuration (maximum MSS/MTU sized packets) the L4-payload rate exceeds the contracted rate....


> In a large ISP I worked with, this went so far that the provider could not sell a 1000 Mbps product if the CPE lacked 2.5G ports, because a 1G physical port simply cannot deliver 1000 Mbps at L3 due to framing overhead.

I could be wrong, but that very much sounds like the situation in Germany. However quite a number of ISPs opted to do exactly that offer nominal 1000 Mbps plans that are limited by Gigabit ethernet ports to actually only deliver around 940 Mbps. The national regulatory agency seems to tolerate this and even baked this into its official method to confirm whether ISPs actually fulfill their contracted rates, as a 10% discount, that is ISPs simply need to deliver >= 90% of the advertised rates as payload rates.



> If a CPE cannot install L3 shapers directly, it needs to internally convert the rate based on its own local stack, accounting for its specific VLAN headers, PPPoE encapsulation, and other overhead.

I disagree, unless the bottleneck operates on L3 (and L2 has ample reserve capacity to absorb the cost on L2-overhead) this will not work out well. A competent shaper needs to faithfully model the true bottleneck, its bottleneck rate, its per-packet overhead and quirky encapsulations like ATM/AAL5, otherwise it will fail to properly shape the traffic in some (probably mot too likely) scenarios. This ID, should in my opinion clearly document and strongly encourage providers to do the right thing here.

comments.author: GIC-de
comments.body: @moeller0 please review changes in https://github.com/GIC-de/draft-dhcp-rate-signaling/pull/13

comments.author: GIC-de
comments.body:
Regarding the rate layer specifically:

- For rates intended to be applied, the Rate Type now indicates the **layer at which the
  enforcement point accounts traffic**. The draft recommends signaling the rate at that layer
  together with the per-packet overhead, and states that a Layer 2 rate with overhead allows
  the most precise modeling of a Layer 2 bottleneck.
- Layer 3 rates remain available where the enforcement point itself accounts at Layer 3, or
  where the applied rate is intended to closely match speed test results, independent of the
  encapsulation on each segment.
- Correction to my earlier comment: the absence of the Rate Type sub-option now means
  *Informational Layer 2 rate*; servers must explicitly signal type 2 or 3 for rates to be
  applied.
- You are right that, with known per-packet overhead, the conversion between layers is exact
  per packet and does not require an average packet size. My argument only applies to
  shapers without per-packet overhead compensation.
- The operational considerations now note that payload-based contracted rates (e.g., per
  BEREC guidelines) are typically met by configuring the enforcement point accordingly, and
  that the signaled values describe the enforcement point, not the contracted payload rate.

Rather than mandating Layer 2 rates, we would like to keep both and let the Rate Type describe
the actual accounting of the enforcement point. Feedback on whether this addresses your
concern is very welcome.

issues.title: Add L2-overhead information
issues.author: moeller0
issues.body:
To properly configure a traffic shaper one needs at least both the true L2-bottleneck rate (or a somewhat lower estimate thereof, e.g. if reporting sync rates of DSL links using PTM the reported rate should be derated for PTM's 64/65 encoding) and the applicable effective per-packet overhead (applicable in that all effective parts are accounted, e.g. ethernet's inter frame gap is not a data, but "radio-silence" worth 12 octets worth of transmission time). As the overhead is hard to deduce even when the true effective bottleneck rate is known, let's add two more mandatory fields to report here downstream and upstream per-packet overhead.
Given the goal of this method is to allow competent CPE-side traffic shaping/scheduling/queue management, let's make sure we mandate the necessary pieces of information to actually make that happen.

comments.author: GIC-de
comments.body:
Thanks a lot for the detailed feedback in #8, #9, and #10. As these issues are closely related,
here is a combined response. The corresponding changes are part of the next revision.

**Per-packet overhead (#9):** We added a *Per-Packet Overhead* sub-option (code 4) carrying:

- a signed **Overhead** (octets accounted per packet in addition to the packet size at the
  signaled layer, as seen by the receiver); where the bottleneck is a physical link, this
  includes physical-layer overhead such as preamble, SFD, and inter-frame gap,
- a **Minimum Packet Unit (MPU)**, and
- **cell-based accounting** parameters (Cell Payload and Cell Size, see #10).

The accounted size of a packet is calculated as `L = max(S + Overhead, MPU)`, followed by
`L = ceil(L / Cell Payload) * Cell Size` if cell-based accounting applies. This maps directly
to shaper parameters such as overhead, mpu, and atm in CAKE.

Sub-option 4 applies to both directions, as the overhead is typically identical and most
clients only apply the upstream rate. Where the overhead differs, an optional *Per-Packet
Overhead Downstream* sub-option (code 5) overrides it for the downstream direction.

PTM 64/65 encoding on VDSL2 and G.fast is expected to be folded into the signaled rate, as you
suggested, with per-packet PTM overhead signaled via the Overhead field.

**Mandatory vs. optional:** We decided to keep the overhead sub-options optional, while
recommending that servers include them (SHOULD) and that receivers with suitable traffic
management functions apply them (SHOULD). Many CPE, including simple script-based
implementations, cannot apply all of these parameters, and we do not want the inability to
apply the overhead to invalidate the rate information itself. Receivers that cannot apply the
overhead may approximate it, e.g., by reducing the applied rate by a margin.

**Examples:** A new appendix provides example values for common deployments: Ethernet link as
bottleneck (Overhead 24, MPU 84), a VLAN tag added by the access node, Layer 3 policers, and
ADSL with PPPoE over bridged LLC/SNAP (Overhead 18, cells 48/53) and PPPoA with VC
multiplexing (Overhead 8, cells 48/53). The values are relative to the Ethernet frame (or PPP
frame) without FCS as seen by the receiver, which is why they differ from the CAKE keywords
that are relative to the IP packet.

Three questions where your input would be very valuable:

1. Are Overhead, MPU, and cell-based accounting sufficient, or are there other effects worth
   covering?
2. Would you be willing to review, or contribute to, the example values in the appendix?
3. Do you see a need to signal both an applied Layer 2 rate and an informational payload rate
   at the same time (e.g., for display in the CPE user interface)? The current format carries
   a single Rate Type per option.

We would appreciate your review of the updated text.

issues.title: Consider adding information about "funky" encapsulations
issues.author: moeller0
issues.body: The canonical example for a quirky encapsulation is ATM/AAL5 that mandates that all data frames are packed into an integer number of ATM cells with the last cell(s) carrying up to 47 bytes of padding. While I hope that no modern encapsulation will ever become that baroque, let's not base the option's utility on my hopes. To solve this we should add a way to signal quirky encapsulations, or maybe relevant encasulations?

comments.author: GIC-de
comments.body:
Rather than an enumeration of encapsulations, which would require a new IANA registry, the
*Per-Packet Overhead* sub-options describe cell-based accounting parametrically with two
fields, **Cell Payload** and **Cell Size**:

- ATM/AAL5 (e.g., ADSL) is signaled as Cell Payload 48 and Cell Size 53, with all
  encapsulation overhead within the AAL5 frame, including the 8-octet AAL5 trailer, carried in
  the Overhead field.
- Any other link layer that pads each packet to an integer number of fixed-size cells can be
  expressed with its own values, without registry changes or an update of the RFC.
- Accounting models that cannot be described by these parameters can be defined as additional
  sub-options in the existing "DHCP Rate Sub-Options" registry (Specification Required), e.g.,
  based on a Broadband Forum specification.

PTM 64/65 on VDSL2 and G.fast is intentionally not modeled as cell-based accounting, as it
encodes a continuous octet stream rather than padding individual packets; its effect is
expected to be folded into the signaled rate.

Feedback on whether this approach covers the "funky" encapsulations you have in mind would be
very welcome.

issues.title: Broaden scope to LAN distribution
issues.author: blocktrron
issues.body:
The concepts focus on the WAN side of a CPE device, but the concept is also useful to apply in a LAN environment to communicate the available WAN bandwidth to a client device.

As a specific use-case, we employ server-side shaping in VPN tunneling applications which primarily cap at CPU capacity of the terminating devices, however this might still be above the WAN bandwidth. Having such a DHCP option available also for LAN is very useful to employ bandwidth limits.

I don't think the concept needs functional changes, however this can be taken into the Problem Statements.
Potentially this case needs clarification in how e.g. a case of a Multi-Gbit WAN and Single-Gbit LAN shall be handled.

comments.author: GIC-de
comments.body: Great point. That’s a very interesting scenario and worth considering in this context.

comments.author: blocktrron
comments.body:
In the LAN case, the meaning needs to be specified more closely to refer to the maximum expected bandwidth for the receiving device.
The current scope does not cover WiFi Hotspot applications where hard shaper limits might be defined per-user. 

Thinking about specific use-cases, communicating this information to client devices can benefit from:

 - Transfer Time Estimations for Downloads
 - Selection of suitable Live Video Quality defaults (Streaming / P2P calls)

comments.author: moeller0
comments.body: Well, any such use would need to be back-stopped by a traffic shaper/policer, especially in the WiFi hotspot case leaving enforcement of limits to the endpoints is inherently abusable/gameable, no?

comments.author: blocktrron
comments.body:
This is not about limit enforcement on the end user device but being able to select the most appropriate configuration for a given experience on the device.

If a smartphone is communicated a connection is able to deliver single digit megabit transfer speeds, it can either auto-select a appropriate resolution / bitrate for live video or can change to mobile data for carrying applications exceeding the LAN capacity.

How this is done is not part of this document, but just ideas which use cases can benefit from this information being available.

comments.author: moeller0
comments.body:
Given that these are at best hints (hard to guarantee the full internet path to arbitrary servers) said smartphone will still need all the methods for automatic rate adjustments, sure, it might start from a higher starting point or it might forego starting at all (but now we opened a DOS channel, or a way to force the use of likely more costly mobile data). For the VPN application it makes some sense to create back-pressure rather earlier than later.
That said, I am all for distributing rate information to the LAN side, so in principle we agree I just want to "kick the tires" on potential examples we could use to motivate this in the draft.

issues.title: Update RFC9445 IANA Registry
issues.author: GIC-de
issues.body:
Alan DeKok suggested that the authors update RFC 9445 and its corresponding IANA registry, "DHCP Options Permitted in the RADIUS DHCPv4-Options Attribute", so this option can be included in a RADIUS Access-Accept packet.

Transmitting this type of configuration from a RADIUS server to devices like a GGSN can be beneficial, as it provides additional mechanisms for signaling bandwidth limits.

pulls.title: Clarify use case, add LAN applicability, and address full review
pulls.author: GIC-de
pulls.body:
## Summary

This PR revises the draft based on feedback from the last IETF presentation and subsequent
mailing list discussions. The main feedback was that the use case was not clear to everyone:
readers who had faced the problem, or had deployed proprietary alternatives, supported the
draft, while others questioned why the CPE needs to know its rate if the BNG already enforces
it, or why shaping is not simply implemented in the BNG. In addition, it was requested to make
the option applicable to LAN environments as well (#11), and to improve the accuracy of rate
signaling for traffic shaping by describing the accounting of the enforcement point, including
per-packet overhead and cell-based link layers (#8, #9, #10).

Besides clarifying the motivation, the PR addresses a full technical and editorial review,
including undefined behaviors, security considerations, RFC compliance, alignment with current
DHCP specifications, and implementability with existing DHCP clients.

## Motivation and Use Case

- **Rewritten Introduction** with a clear structure: *Problem Statement*, *Solution Overview*,
  and *Applicability*.
- **Problem Statement** now explains the actual mechanism:
  - Upstream rates are commonly enforced by **ingress policers** at the BNG, as per-subscriber
    upstream queuing is not supported by all BNG platforms or only with restrictions and
    reduced scale. A CPE sending at line rate causes policer drops, sawtooth throughput, and
    poor speed test results.
  - Other upstream bottlenecks: access devices (ONT, DSL modem, cable modem) and limitations
    within the access network (PON upstream allocation, DSL synchronization rate, cable modem
    rate limits).
  - Upstream **prioritization at the CPE** (DNS, VoIP, gaming, video conferencing, TCP ACKs,
    selected clients) is ineffective unless the CPE is the bottleneck.
  - Downstream rates are mainly informational for the CPE but relevant for intermediate nodes.
- **Solution Overview** with a figure showing upstream policing with and without CPE shaping.
  BNG enforcement remains in place; the CPE shaper prevents it from being triggered.
- **New Appendix "Design Rationale"** addressing frequently raised questions: why BNG
  enforcement alone is not sufficient, why upstream shaping is not performed at the BNG
  (including NAT limitations), why not TR-069 or manual configuration, why DHCP, and the
  limitations of existing proprietary solutions, while CPE implementations already provide
  Layer 2 and Layer 3 shaping functions.
- **Abstract** rewritten accordingly, including intermediate nodes and LAN applicability.

## LAN Applicability (closes #11)

- New section *Local Area Networks* under *Deployment Scenarios*: use cases (VPN gateways,
  Wi-Fi hotspots with per-user limits, applications using the rates as initial estimate),
  propagation of WAN rates to LAN clients, recommendation of informational rate types for
  shared capacity, and the requirement that clients do not use signaled rates as a replacement
  for congestion control.
- Direction definitions (*Upstream*, *Downstream*) are now relative to the interface on which
  the option is received, independent of broadband terminology.

## Rate Types and Per-Packet Overhead (refs #8, #9, #10)

- **Rate Types:** type 1 is now *Informational Layer 3 rate*. Absence of the Rate Type
  sub-option means *Informational Layer 2 rate*; servers must explicitly signal type 2 or 3
  for rates to be applied. Precise Layer 2 rate definition (VLAN tags and PPPoE headers
  included; FCS, preamble, SFD, and IPG excluded).
- For applied rates, the Rate Type indicates the **layer at which the enforcement point
  accounts traffic**, so that receivers can model this accounting. New term *Enforcement
  Point*.
- **Layer 3 rates** closely correspond to speed test results and are identical on every node,
  independent of encapsulation; receivers shaping at a lower layer compensate for the headers
  implicitly.
- **New optional *Per-Packet Overhead* sub-options:** code 4 applies to both directions, code
  5 overrides it for downstream. Each carries a signed overhead (including physical-layer
  overhead such as preamble, SFD, and IPG where the bottleneck is a physical link), a minimum
  packet unit (MPU), and parametric **cell-based accounting** (cell payload and cell size,
  e.g., 48/53 for ATM/AAL5 on ADSL), without requiring an additional registry. The parameters
  map directly to shaper parameters such as those of CAKE.
- Receivers that cannot apply the overhead, fully or partially, still apply the signaled
  rates; the option remains valid.
- Guidance on applying rates at a different accounting layer, on PPPoE interfaces, and on
  VDSL2 PTM encapsulation.
- **New Appendix with example parameter values** for Ethernet links, VLAN tags added by the
  access node, Layer 3 policers, and ADSL with PPPoE over LLC/SNAP and PPPoA.
- Rate Type section restructured into format, definitions, semantics, and server and
  receiver guidance.

## Protocol Changes and Clarifications

- **New section *Rate Processing*:** deliberately stateless processing that can be implemented
  by simple DHCP client hook scripts:
  - the last valid OPTION_RATE wins, regardless of DHCPv4 or DHCPv6, maintained per interface;
  - an absent rate sub-option or a value of 0 resets that direction;
  - a message without OPTION_RATE leaves the applied rates unchanged;
  - rates are not bound to the lease; they are reset when the link or session is terminated;
  - no reconfiguration if rates, rate type, and overhead are unchanged;
  - optional correction factor for intermediate nodes (e.g., +1%) so that CPE shaping does not
    trigger enforcement, while non-supporting CPE are still policed.
- **New section *Client Hints*:** hints indicate client capacity; honoring a hint can only
  lower the signaled rate. Relays and snooping devices must not use client-supplied values.
- **Error Handling:** length validation, malformed option handling, multiple instances
  (RFC 3396 concatenation for DHCPv4), sub-option codes 0 and 255 reserved, shared 0-255 code
  space for DHCPv4 and DHCPv6.
- **Server behavior:** aligned for DHCPv4 and DHCPv6; explicit rules for removing previously
  signaled rates; DHCPFORCERENEW (RFC 3203/6704) and Reconfigure (with RKAP) for mid-lease
  updates; DSL actual line rate guidance.
- **Relay agent behavior:** DHCPv6 relays process only their own Relay-reply; optional
  zero-length OPTION_RATE in Relay-forward as support indication; devices modifying the
  client's option act as server or proxy; trusted-port processing for Layer 2 relays and
  snooping devices.
- **Assumption of one client per physical or logical port** for intermediate nodes.
- **New Appendix "Example Receiver Processing"** summarizing the complete processing as
  pseudocode for implementers.

## Security, Privacy, and Operations

- Security Considerations extended: all signaling paths, DHCP snooping / DHCPv6-Shield,
  configurable minimum rate sanity checks, removal of rate limits, excessive overhead values,
  resource exhaustion on intermediate nodes, unauthenticated client hints, rogue servers in
  LANs.
- New *Privacy Considerations* section (RFC 7844, fingerprinting via hints).
- Operational Considerations extended: choice of rate type and overhead, payload-based
  contracted rates, VDSL2 PTM, correction factors, actual line rates, update latency, and
  measuring client support.
- New *Implementation Status* section (RFC 7942) including a feasibility analysis for OpenWrt
  (udhcpc, odhcp6c, dnsmasq, odhcpd, CAKE) without changes to the DHCP client software.

## IANA and References

- Category changed to **Standards Track**.
- Registries use **Specification Required**, allowing e.g. Broadband Forum TRs as
  specifications; DHCP Rate Types registry restored; Designated Expert guidelines extended.
- New sub-options *Per-Packet Overhead* (code 4) and *Per-Packet Overhead Downstream*
  (code 5); no additional registries.
- DHCPv6 option registration includes *Client ORO* and *Singleton Option*.
- RFC 8415 replaced by **RFC 9915** (no technical impact; section numbers unchanged).
- New references: RFC 2364, 2684, 3203, 3396, 4649, 6704, 7227, 7610, 7844, 7942,
  IEEE 802.1Q, IEEE 802.3; corrected TR-069 reference.
- Justification for the use of sub-options with respect to RFC 7227.

## Editorial

- Additional discussion venue (broadband@ietf.org) moved into the venue section, so it is
  removed by the RFC Editor, with proper links.
- Consistent RFC 9915 message names and IEEE 802.3 terminology, neutral IETF wording (removed
  promotional language), consistent terminology (client-facing, Layer 2 DHCPv4 Relay Agent,
  Receiver, Enforcement Point).
- Body restructured: *Error Handling* moved next to *Rate Processing*, *PPPoE* and *Local Area
  Networks* grouped under *Deployment Scenarios*, *Interaction with AQM and L4S* merged into
  the Introduction.

## Review Notes

- Large diff due to restructuring; reviewing the rendered HTML is recommended.
- Feedback is particularly welcome on the Introduction and the Design Rationale appendix, as
  they address the main concerns raised during the last presentation, and on the
  *Per-Packet Overhead* sub-options and the example values (#8, #9, #10).
